intro_html: Stifado is the Greek stew where the onions are not a background note, they are half the dish. They cook down until they melt into a sweet and sour braise sharpened with red wine vinegar and warmed with allspice and nutmeg. Beef chuck goes in tough and comes out shredding. Each bowl carries 622 calories and 44 grams of protein for about $6.90 a serving (at everyday cost).
cost_closing_html: About $6.90 a bowl (at everyday cost), and nearly all of it is the beef. Everything else in this pot is onions, vinegar, and canned tomato, which is about as cheap as flavor gets.
shop_smart: Buy the onions in a big bag, not loose. This recipe uses more onion than any other dish on the site, and the bag price per pound is always better than the single price.

Chuck roast is the only expensive line here. It is also the correct cut, because the collagen in it is what turns the sauce silky over a long simmer. A leaner cut costs more and gives you a worse stew.
Red wine vinegar is a pantry bottle that lasts through many batches, so the sting of buying it lands once and pays out over months.
Canned diced tomatoes plus a spoonful of tomato paste do the same job as a whole tray of fresh tomatoes for a fraction of the money, and they hold their flavor through a two-hour braise.
make_it: Weigh your empty mixing pot and write the number down for portioning later.
Cut the chuck into big chunks, dry them well, and season with salt and pepper. Brown them hard in olive oil in batches, then set them aside. Do not rush this part, and do not crowd the pan.
Peel the onions and cut them into thick wedges. Add them to the pot with the rest of the oil and cook over medium heat until they soften and start to color, about 20 minutes.
Pour in the red wine vinegar and let it bubble down while you scrape every brown bit off the bottom of the pot. That fond is the backbone of the sauce.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook it for a minute, then add the diced tomatoes, beef broth, chicken broth, bay leaves, allspice, and nutmeg.
Return the beef, bring it to a bare simmer, cover, and leave it alone for about 2 hours. Stifado does not want to be stirred every five minutes. The onions need to be left in peace to collapse.
Uncover for the last 20 minutes so the sauce reduces and thickens around the meat. Pull the bay leaves out, taste for salt, and add a splash more vinegar if it needs brightening.
portion_html: Set the full pot on the scale, subtract the empty-pot weight you wrote down, and divide by 14. Scoop to that gram target and every container lands at 622 calories with an even share of the beef, which is the part that actually matters. Stifado gets better as it sits, so the last container of the week is the best one you will eat.

head.description: Greek stifado, a sweet and sour beef and onion braise with vinegar and allspice, rebuilt for 14 meal prep servings at about $6.90 a bowl (at everyday cost).
head.keywords: greek stifado, beef and onion stew, mosharaki stifado, beef chuck braise, greek meal prep, budget beef stew, high protein meal prep
recipeIngredient: Pantry: bay leaves, ground allspice, ground nutmeg, salt, black pepper
steps: Season and brown the beef chunks in olive oil in batches, then set aside.
Cook the onion wedges in the same pot until soft and lightly colored.
Deglaze with red wine vinegar, scraping the bottom, then stir in the tomato paste.
Add the tomatoes, both broths, bay leaves, allspice, and nutmeg, then return the beef.
Cover and simmer about 2 hours, uncovering at the end to thicken the sauce.
Weigh the pot and divide into 14 containers.
